correctness.rationale: The frozen statement is mathematically correct. Downsampling the positive second-difference measure with the factor t^κ(1+⋯+t^{p−1})² gives the second-difference moments for the block sequence. If q=d²≠1, the first three of these moments force zero variance at t^p=q. If q=1, the total mass is zero. The original measure can therefore have only the indicated positive atom (no positive atom in the unit case), and it can have a zero atom only for κ>0. Solving the resulting recurrence and matching the geometric subsequence eliminates the affine part in the nonunit case and the slope in the unit case. The equation at n=0 forces c≤1 and gives exactly the stated two-point Berger measure; κ=0 gives c=1. For sharpness, the two positive masses C(u−1)² and D(v−1)² have sum (q−1)² and first moment q(q−1)², so matching γ_0 and γ_p yields γ_{jp}=q^j for j≤3. The positive variance gives γ_{4p}>q⁴. The coefficient limits yield positivity and bounded consecutive ratios for each fixed p. This is an exact check, not a finite test.
